the depth distribution of Calanus finmargicus was best explained by biotic factors in neritic and open ocean environments, with the exception of a small area in the oceanic environment, which was characterized by a high abundance of C. fin- marchicus and where depth distribution was best explained by the abiotic factor depth of the pycnolcline.

the ecology of marine zooplakton in the North Atlantic.
the ecology of the marine copepod, Calanus finmargicus, and its role in the marine ecosystem, with special focus on the Subarctic region.
the habitat selection of marine zooplakton in a highly fluctuating ocean environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the copepod C. finm- archicus is an opportunistic species, which selects its habitat based on food availability, and that it does not perform a diel vertical migration.

C. finm- archicus selects its habitat (depth) dynamically based on food conditions (phytoplankton biomass) and predation pressure (copepod density), and that this habitat choice is similar in neritic as in oceanic areas.
the copepods were not migrating vertically but were selecting their depth of occurrence based on food conditions, predation risk and other biotic and abiotic factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
C. finm- archicus in the Subarctics seems to be a “sit-and-wait” predator.
the depth of C. fin- marchicus in the Subarctics is best predicted by the density of the species, which in turn is best predicted by food conditions (chlorophyll a).
copepods are not just passive agents carried by currents and tides, but rather they have a strong capacity to select habitat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the depth distribution of zooplankton is not only a function of physical factors but is also influenced by biotic factors.
zooplankton may select their habitat based on the food conditions and predators.
the distribution of C. finmachicus was not determined by abiotic factors alone, but also by biotic interactions, such as food availability and predation risk.
